text.p: Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri has ordered an investigation into charges by a former prime minister that equipment for intercepting cellular telephone calls has recently been installed in Lebanon.
Hariri asked Defence Minister Mohsen Dalloul in a letter on Tuesday to look into the allegations made on March 15 by Selim al-Hoss, a parliamentary deputy who has twice been prime minister.

Hoss said in a parliamentary question that: "It has come to our knowledge that a device for tapping cellular telephone calls has been installed about one month ago to complement the existing wire-tapping operation."

Lebanon's two cellular networks have grown rapidly since their introduction in 1994. They now have some 200,000 subscribers and rival the normal telephone network which is still being repaired after the 1975-90 civil war.

Hariri asked Dalloul to inform him of measures he would take "in case any (security) organ attached directly to your ministry, or any official administration is proved to be involved in tapping regular and cellular telephones."

The government, which has repeatedly been accused by opposition politicians of illegal wiretapping, has two weeks to reply to Hoss's question. Wiretapping is only permitted in Lebanon on authorisation of a judge.
Officials at Libancell and Cellis, the two cellular telephone companies operating in Lebanon which were set up by Finland Telecom and France Telecom, have said they are not aware of any wiretapping.

Government officials also say no wiretapping takes place in Lebanon but according to Beirut newspapers Lebanese security services have long had the ability to intercept calls on the normal telephone network.
